---
title: "Scattered data"
engine: julia
---

```{julia}
#| echo: false
using ConvolutionInterpolations, CairoMakie, Printf, Random
rms(v) = sqrt(sum(abs2, v) / length(v));                  # root mean square, used throughout
```

Measurements rarely come on a grid. The Julia package handles scattered points by fitting a
grid to them: a convolution interpolant on a grid over the points' bounding box, whose knot
values are chosen so that the interpolant matches the points. The result is an ordinary gridded
interpolant, so everything on the other pages — evaluation anywhere, derivatives, integrals —
works on it unchanged. `fit_scattered` does the fit and returns the grid;
`convolution_interpolation(points, values)` does the fit and returns the interpolant.

The Python port does not include scattered data yet; the [feature matrix](../features.qmd)
tracks the port.

## Two modes

- `mode = :smooth`, the default, smooths: it minimises the misfit at the points plus a
  roughness penalty whose weight is chosen by generalized cross-validation, and reports the
  noise level it found. For measured data, which carry noise.
- `mode = :exact` interpolates: the fit passes through every point to machine precision, and
  among the grids that do, the smoothest is chosen. For trusted, noise-free data only — noise
  would be reproduced exactly and amplified between the points.

The default differs from the gridded constructors, which always interpolate, because
scattered data are usually measurements.

## Noisy measurements

Points in the unit square, one per column of the matrix, with a smooth signal and noise:

```{julia}
Random.seed!(1)                                           # reproducible points and noise
pts = rand(2, 800)                                        # 800 scattered points in 2D, one per column
signal(x, y) = sin(3x) * cos(2y)                          # the signal
σ = 0.05                                                  # the noise standard deviation
vals = [signal(p[1], p[2]) for p in eachcol(pts)]         # the signal at the points
noisy = vals .+ σ .* randn(800)                           # measured with noise

itp = convolution_interpolation(pts, noisy)               # the interpolant, smoothing chosen by cross-validation
knots, grid, info = fit_scattered(pts, noisy)             # the same fit, returned as its grid and the fit's report
info                                                      # the smoothing parameter and the estimated noise
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
x1, x2 = extrema(pts[1, :])                               # the fit's domain is the points' bounding box
y1, y2 = extrema(pts[2, :])
xf = range(x1, x2, length = 150)                          # a fine grid over it, for measuring the error
yf = range(y1, y2, length = 150)
itp_fine = [itp(xi, yi) for xi in xf, yi in yf]           # the interpolant on it
exact2 = [signal(xi, yi) for xi in xf, yi in yf]          # the signal on it
println("| | the noisy points | the fitted interpolant |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| rms error against the signal | %.4f | %.4f |\n", rms(noisy .- vals), rms(itp_fine .- exact2))
println()
println("| | generated | estimated by the fit |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| noise standard deviation | %.4f | %.4f |\n", σ, info.noise)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
fig = Figure(size = (800, 400))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; title = "interpolant", aspect = DataAspect())
heatmap!(ax1, xf, yf, itp_fine; colorrange = (-1, 1))
scatter!(ax1, pts[1, :], pts[2, :]; markersize = 3, color = :white, strokecolor = :black, strokewidth = 0.5)
ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; title = "signal", aspect = DataAspect())
heatmap!(ax2, xf, yf, exact2; colorrange = (-1, 1))
fig
```

The grid is sized from the point density, as fine as the points resolve, and the smoothing is
set by the penalty weight, not by the knot count; the [smoothing page](smoothing.qmd) compares
this fit with Gaussian smoothing on gridded data.

## Trusted data

With `mode = :exact` the interpolant passes through the points. Since it is a gridded
interpolant underneath, its derivatives and integrals come from the same object; the wrapper
forwards `derivative`, so a box integral over the points' domain is four evaluations of the
twofold antiderivative:

```{julia}
Random.seed!(2)
pts2 = rand(2, 300)                                       # 300 trusted points
vals2 = [signal(p[1], p[2]) for p in eachcol(pts2)]       # the signal, without noise

itp_x = convolution_interpolation(pts2, vals2; mode = :exact)                      # interpolates the points
dx_x  = convolution_interpolation(pts2, vals2; mode = :exact, derivative = (1, 0)) # ∂/∂x of the same fit
ii_x  = convolution_interpolation(pts2, vals2; mode = :exact, derivative = (-1, -1)) # ∫∫ from the corner

box = (0.2, 0.7, 0.3, 0.8)                                # x₁, x₂, y₁, y₂ of a box inside the domain
boxint(F, x1, x2, y1, y2) = F(x2, y2) - F(x1, y2) - F(x2, y1) + F(x1, y1)   # inclusion–exclusion
itp_x(0.4, 0.6), dx_x(0.4, 0.6), boxint(ii_x, box...)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
exact_box = (cos(3 * 0.2) - cos(3 * 0.7)) / 3 * (sin(2 * 0.8) - sin(2 * 0.3)) / 2   # ∫∫ sin(3x)cos(2y) over the box
println("| | f(0.4, 0.6) | ∂f/∂x (0.4, 0.6) | ∫∫ over the box |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
@printf("| from the fit | %.8f | %.8f | %.8f |\n", itp_x(0.4, 0.6), dx_x(0.4, 0.6), boxint(ii_x, box...))
@printf("| exact | %.8f | %.8f | %.8f |\n", signal(0.4, 0.6), 3cos(3 * 0.4) * cos(2 * 0.6), exact_box)
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
viol = maximum(abs(itp_x(p[1], p[2]) - v) for (p, v) in zip(eachcol(pts2), vals2))   # the fit at the points
@printf("The largest deviation of the interpolant from the data at the points is %.1e.\n", viol)
```

## Clustered points and adaptive grids

`grid = :adaptive` lets the fit place its knots instead of spacing them evenly, and the two
modes place them differently. In `:smooth` mode the knots follow the fitted surface: a first
fit on the uniform grid gives the curvature, the knots of each axis are spread so that each
interval carries the same share of it, and the fit is repeated on those knots, so a steep
layer or a sharp bump gets the knots it needs and flat regions give theirs up. In `:exact`
mode the knots follow the points: an exact fit needs the grid to separate the points, two
points in one grid cell cannot both be matched, and a uniform grid sized from the mean density
cannot do that for clustered points — the fit then says so with a warning and returns the
least-squares fit instead. The adaptive grid places the knots of each axis at the quantiles of
the points' coordinates, so a dense band of points gets a dense band of knots, and where the
points are dense because the function varies fast there, as in a measurement campaign that
samples a layer closely, the dense knots are also where the accuracy is needed:

```{julia}
layer(x) = tanh(40x)                                      # a steep layer at the centre
u = range(-1, 1, length = 60)
xs = sign.(u) .* abs.(u) .^ 2                             # 60 points, clustered towards the layer
pts1 = reshape(xs, 1, :)                                  # as a 1 × n matrix
ys = layer.(xs)                                           # trusted values

ku, vu, viol_u = fit_scattered(pts1, ys; mode = :exact)                    # uniform grid: warns
ka, va, viol_a = fit_scattered(pts1, ys; mode = :exact, grid = :adaptive)  # adaptive grid
itp_u = convolution_interpolation(ku, vu; kernel = :b5, bc = :poly)        # the kernel the fit used
itp_a = convolution_interpolation(ka, va; kernel = :b5);                   # a nonuniform grid: the nonuniform :b5 kernel
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
xr = range(-1, 1, length = 1001)
itp_d = convolution_interpolation(collect(xs), ys; kernel = :b5)   # for comparison: the nonuniform kernel with its knots at the points
println("| | uniform grid | adaptive grid | knots at the points |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
@printf("| knots | %d | %d | %d |\n", length(ku[1]), length(ka[1]), length(xs))
@printf("| largest deviation at the points | %.1e | %.1e | %.1e |\n", viol_u, viol_a, maximum(abs.(itp_d.(xs) .- ys)))
@printf("| largest error against the function | %.1e | %.1e | %.1e |\n", maximum(abs.(itp_u.(xr) .- layer.(xr))), maximum(abs.(itp_a.(xr) .- layer.(xr))), maximum(abs.(itp_d.(xr) .- layer.(xr))))
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
fig = Figure(size = (800, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "x")
scatter!(ax, xs, ys; markersize = 10, color = :white, strokecolor = :black, strokewidth = 1.5, label = "points")
lines!(ax, xr, itp_u.(xr); label = "uniform grid")
lines!(ax, xr, itp_a.(xr); label = "adaptive grid")
lines!(ax, xr, layer.(xr); color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "function")
scatter!(ax, ka[1], fill(-1.1, length(ka[1])); marker = :vline, markersize = 12, color = :black, label = "adaptive knots")
Legend(fig[1, 2], ax)
fig
```

Exactness at the points and accuracy between them are different things. On the same clustered
points sampled from a function that is smooth everywhere, the uniform fit's least-squares
compromise is as accurate as the adaptive fit's exact match, often more so, because the
uniform grid spends its knots evenly where the function needs them evenly. The adaptive grid
pays off when the points are dense where the function is steep, or when the values themselves
must be reproduced. The last column of the table is the nonuniform kernel with its knots at
the points — the plain interpolant through the same samples. The fit is more accurate than
that as well: among the grids that match the points it takes the smoothest, and the knots it
has between the points serve that end.

An adaptive grid is nonuniform, so the interpolant on it is the nonuniform one of the
[nonuniform page](nonuniform.qmd): derivatives are available, antiderivatives are not. The
spacing ratio of adjacent knots is capped by the `ratio` keyword, which keeps the nonuniform
kernels well conditioned; raise it for strongly graded data. The grid is still a tensor
product, so it helps when the point density is roughly separable along the axes — a boundary
layer, a log-scaled axis — and not for isolated clusters.

## Knots and points

Two keywords size the grid. `oversample` is the number of knots per mean point spacing, with
mode-dependent defaults (lower for `:smooth`, where the penalty does the regularising; higher
for `:exact` in two or more dimensions, where random points share cells more often);
`gridsize` fixes the knot count outright. Both modes warn when the grid is the limit: `:exact`
when the points could not all be matched, `:smooth` when the fitted smoothing would need a
finer grid than the budget allows.

A third keyword, `bc`, sets the boundary rule of a `:smooth` fit on a uniform grid, as for the
gridded interpolants on the [boundaries page](boundaries.qmd): `:poly`, the default, fits the
kernel's full polynomial at each end, and `:quadratic` or `:linear` fit a lower degree. The
default is the more accurate where the signal is steep at an end; where the data are flat at
an end and noisy, the lower-degree rules are the remedy for an end that wanders. The rule can
differ between the two ends of an axis, as a pair `(:poly, :linear)`, and between axes.

A fourth keyword, `q`, is the order of the roughness that both modes minimise, and it is what
"smoothest" means on this page. Roughness is measured by the `q`-th differences of the knot
values; the default is 5, except for an exact fit in one dimension, where it follows the
kernel. From two dimensions up the two modes measure it differently. `:smooth` takes the
differences along each axis. `:exact` takes every difference of total order `q`, the mixed
ones across the axes included, which treats all directions alike. That is the measure the
polyharmonic splines minimise, and it decides what the fit does in the gaps between the
points, where most of the grid lies in several dimensions. It favours features without a
preferred direction: for a signal that is a product of one-dimensional factors, differences
along the axes would be the better measure, and the exact fit is somewhat less accurate there.

## Solving an exact fit

An exact fit is the smoothest grid that passes through the points, and the `solver` keyword
chooses how it is found. `:cholesky` factorizes a sparse system in the knot values. It is
cheap in one and two dimensions, but from three on the factorization fills in, and its memory
and time grow steeply with the grid. `:dual` finds the grid of `:cholesky`, to within the
tolerance of its iteration, from a dense system with one unknown per data point, so its cost
follows the number of points and not the grid, which is what makes exact fits practical in
four dimensions and above. `:qr` is a slower sparse
least-squares solve that lowers the roundoff floor of the wide kernels; it is for chasing the
last digits with `kernel = :b7`, and its memory limits it to small grids from three
dimensions up.

The default, `solver = :auto`, uses `:cholesky` in one and two dimensions and `:dual` from
three. `:dual` needs a uniform grid, `Float64` data, and more points than there are
polynomials of total degree below `q`, so an adaptive grid, `BigFloat` data or a handful of
points stay with `:cholesky` in any dimension. The dense system of `:dual` takes 8 bytes per
pair of points; before using it, `:auto` checks that it fits in the machine's memory and
raises an error if it does not, while `solver = :dual` given explicitly is used unchecked.
Duplicated points are the other limit: `:cholesky` resolves conflicting values in the
least-squares sense, while `:dual` warns, and the returned violation shows that the data were
not reproduced.

The two solvers on the same thousand trusted points in three dimensions:

```{julia}
Random.seed!(3)
f3(x, y, z) = sin(3x) * cos(2y) * exp(-z)                 # a smooth signal in three dimensions
pts3 = rand(3, 1000)                                      # 1000 trusted points in the unit cube
vals3 = [f3(p...) for p in eachcol(pts3)]                 # the signal at the points

warm = (pts3[:, 1:200], vals3[1:200])                     # a small fit compiles each solver,
fit_scattered(warm...; mode = :exact, solver = :cholesky) # so that the timings below
fit_scattered(warm...; mode = :exact, solver = :dual)     # measure the solve alone

res_c = @timed fit_scattered(pts3, vals3; mode = :exact, solver = :cholesky)   # sparse, grid unknowns
res_d = @timed fit_scattered(pts3, vals3; mode = :exact, solver = :dual)       # dense, point unknowns
(kc, vc, viol_c), (kd, vd, viol_d) = res_c.value, res_d.value;                 # knots, values, violation
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
println("| | `:cholesky` | `:dual` |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| time (s) | %.2f | %.2f |\n", res_c.time, res_d.time)
@printf("| allocated (GB) | %.2f | %.2f |\n", res_c.bytes / 2^30, res_d.bytes / 2^30)
@printf("| largest deviation at the points | %.1e | %.1e |\n", viol_c, viol_d)
println()
@printf("The two grids differ by at most %.1e relative to the largest knot value.\n",
        maximum(abs, vc .- vd) / maximum(abs, vc))
```

The [scattered-data benchmark](../benchmarks/julia/scattered.qmd) compares both modes with
the radial basis function and natural-neighbour packages on accuracy, time, and what the fit
returns that they do not.
